strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: estimating deployed classifier performance when target labels are unavailable. Combining density-ratio weighting with score calibration is intuitive and does not require retraining the monitored classifier.

The evaluation is substantial within its domain: 959 dataset-model cases and 36,557 production chunks across five Folktables tasks and five classifiers. Table 1 reports improvements over importance weighting on all six evaluation measures, including F1 MASTE decreasing from 1.06 to 0.91.

Using the same density-ratio estimator for IW and PAPE, alongside unweighted calibration through CBPE, provides useful component comparisons. Public datasets, temporal splits, computational information, and a linked code repository support reproducibility.

Section 3.3 explicitly acknowledges concept shift, support mismatch, calibration error, and sampling uncertainty. These are useful disclosures. No material ethical concern is apparent from the reported public-data experiments.
weaknesses: The central claim of supporting any performance metric is not established. Equations (1)–(2) cover expectations of per-example quantities, whereas F1 is a nonlinear ratio and AUROC requires pairwise comparisons. For example, an always-positive classifier at 50% prevalence has population F1 of 2/3, while averaging its single-example F1 values gives 1/2. Metric-specific estimators and derivations are missing for two of the three headline metrics, leaving a major gap between the algorithm, theory, and experiments.

The theoretical support is narrower than advertised. Equation (4) incorrectly equates conditional mean absolute label residual with absolute calibration bias; the former can remain positive under perfect calibration. The subsequent calibration-bias bound is repairable, but the analysis assumes an accurate target calibrator and does not establish how errors in the estimated density ratios and fitted calibrator affect the implemented procedure.

Key implementation details are absent from the manuscript, particularly the density-ratio classifier and weighted calibrator families, their hyperparameters, preprocessing, and regularization. Algorithm 1 fits the domain classifier and evaluates reference weights on the same observations without explaining how overfitting is controlled. The repository link is helpful, but the manuscript alone does not adequately specify the central estimator.

Experimental breadth is limited despite the large case count: every case comes from the same census data source. There are no controlled covariate-shift experiments separating estimator error from violations of the assumed invariant label conditional, and the sample-size analysis covers only one selected case. These omissions limit conclusions about robustness and explainability of the observed gains.

The statistical evidence needs more careful reporting. The Wilcoxon result is given as p = 0.0 without specifying the pairing unit or treatment of dependence among chunks and models sharing data. Chunk-weighted aggregates favor cases with more observations, while case-level improvement distributions and uncertainty estimates are missing. This matters particularly for the relatively modest accuracy and AUROC gains over IW.

Originality is insufficiently distinguished from established density-ratio estimation, importance-weighted calibration, and conditional-expectation performance estimation. The manuscript cites prior calibration-transfer work but does not clearly identify a new theoretical principle or characterize when its combination improves upon IW. The empirical contribution is promising, but the technical and reporting gaps prevent it from carrying the acceptance case.

The abstract overstates the method's access requirements and assumptions: Algorithm 1 requires reference and production features, beyond predictions and probability estimates, and validity requires covariate shift and support overlap. These claims should be aligned with the more careful limitations section.
